description:
We’re a Kenyan team from Tafiti R&I Hub building PumpPay: a locally made solar pump controller with a pay-as-you-go app that helps smallholder farmers water their crops smarter. 

For the Field Shift challenge, we’re making it smarter. It will use NASA POWER weather and solar data to decide when to pump and how much water each crop needs, check soil health from satellite soil maps, recommend what to plant next, and share solar power between the pump, the battery, and the home.
summary:
Smallholders grow up to 80% of sub-Saharan Africa’s food, yet only 1.7% of Kenya’s farmland is irrigated, and farmers who can pump still guess when and how much to water.

PumpPay is a solar pump controller made in Kenya, with a pay-as-you-go app that turns NASA satellite data into one clear daily instruction for each field. Daily NASA POWER data on sunshine, temperature, humidity, wind, rainfall and root-zone soil moisture runs the FAO-56 crop water model for 12 crops. The app tells farmers how many litres to pump, timed to the sunniest hours of the forecast. It also scores soil health from global soil maps and recommends what to plant next.

Farmers pay by M-Pesa and the pump unlocks in seconds. A voice assistant answers in English and Kiswahili, and the app works offline at the pump.

PumpPay replaces guesswork and diesel with precise, affordable irrigation, keeps soil healthy season after season, and helps open more of Kenya’s 1.34 million hectares of irrigation potential, only 16% of which is developed. What sets it apart is that it joins NASA data, a locally built controller and mobile payments in one system.
details:
What it does
PumpPay is a solar irrigation system for smallholder farms, made in Kenya. It has three parts: a solar pump controller we designed and built, an Android app, and a cloud backend. Together, they decide when the pump should run and for how long, using NASA satellite data, and let farmers pay for pumping through M-Pesa as they go.

How it works

1. The controller. An ESP32-based controller, on a circuit board we designed in KiCad, sits between the solar panels and the pump. It measures the pump’s voltage, current, and power and its own temperature, records run time hour by hour, and switches the pump on and off. It keeps track of paid pumping time on the board itself, so the pump keeps working with no signal and locks when the credit runs out. It talks to the phone over Bluetooth and sends readings to the cloud over WiFi.

2. The watering decision. For the farm’s exact location, the backend downloads 21 days of NASA POWER daily data: maximum and minimum temperature, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation, rainfall, and root-zone soil wetness. It calculates how much water the crop loses each day with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method, adjusted for the crop’s stage of growth, and tracks how much water is left in the root zone, starting from NASA’s soil wetness reading. When the soil dries past the crop’s stress point, it works out the water needed, in litres for that field and in minutes for that pump. NASA POWER data runs a few days behind, so the model carries the balance forward to today and says so.

3. Timing to the sun. A solar pump without a battery only runs well in strong sunshine. The app reads the OpenWeather 5-day forecast, estimates the sunshine every half hour from the sun’s position and the forecast cloud cover, and picks the sunniest stretch of the day for pumping. When enough rain is forecast, the pump stays off. It also turns the forecast into plain farm advice: rain, heat, wind for spraying, and damp weather that spreads crop disease.

4. Soil health. From the farm’s pin, the app reads the ISRIC SoilGrids soil map (250 m detail): acidity (pH), organic carbon, nitrogen, nutrient-holding capacity and soil texture. It turns these into a score out of 100, with one piece of advice for each part. A farmer’s own soil test replaces the map’s estimate. Because the controller records how long the pump ran, the app also compares the water applied with what the crop used, and flags over-watering, which washes nitrogen below the roots, as well as under-watering.

5. What to plant next. The app keeps each field’s crop history and ranks 12 crops for the next season. It uses crop rotation rules (change the crop family, follow a hungry crop with a legume, change the root depth), the soil’s acidity and nitrogen, and the coming season’s rain and temperature from NASA POWER’s 25-year climate record, adjusted to the farm’s altitude using NASA SRTM elevation data. It also checks whether the pump can supply the crop’s peak water demand. The farmer gets a top pick, two alternatives, crops to leave out, and a three-season plan.

6. The assistant. Farmers can ask questions by voice or text, in English or Kiswahili. The assistant answers with the same numbers the app shows, and offers one-tap buttons, for example, to save a field size or open the soil page.

7. Paying. Farmers top up through M-Pesa from the app, and the pump unlocks within seconds. They can pay daily towards owning the system (pay as you go), or pay only for the hours they pump (pay as you use).

Benefits

  • One clear instruction instead of guesswork: how many litres, how many minutes, and the best time to pump.
  • Water and fertiliser go further, because the crop gets what it needs and no more.
  • No diesel, and no high upfront cost.
  • Healthier soil over time, through crop rotation and better watering.
  • It works at the pump without mobile data, over Bluetooth.

Intended impact
Smallholders grow up to 80% of the food in sub-Saharan Africa (IFAD), yet only 1.7% of Kenya’s farmland is irrigated (Kenya National Irrigation Policy, 2017), and only 16% of Kenya’s 1.34 million hectares of irrigation potential has been developed (National Irrigation Services Strategy). We want to make irrigation affordable and precise for these farmers: more harvests a year, steadier incomes, less wasted water and fertiliser, and soils that stay productive. Our next steps are field pilots with farmers to measure water saved and yields gained, a flow meter so litres are measured rather than estimated, and sharing solar power between the pump, a battery, and the home.

Tools and technologies

  • Hardware: ESP32 microcontroller, relay switching, voltage and current sensing, a 20x2 character display with four buttons, a circuit board designed in KiCad, and our own enclosure design.
  • Firmware: C++ (Arduino framework).
  • Mobile app: Kotlin with Jetpack Compose for Android; Bluetooth; Leaflet maps stored in the app for offline use; Android speech recognition and text-to-speech.
  • Backend: Firebase (Cloud Functions on Node.js, Firestore, Authentication with Google sign-in, Secret Manager) and the M-Pesa Daraja API.
  • AI: a large language model (gpt-oss-120b, served by Groq), called only from our server and grounded on our own model results.
  • Data: NASA POWER (daily data and climate averages), NASA SRTM elevation (through OpenTopoData), ISRIC SoilGrids, and the OpenWeather forecast.
  • Methods: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith and Hargreaves, FAO-56 crop coefficients and soil water balance, the USDA soil texture triangle, and established clear-sky and cloud-cover sunshine models.
  • Testing: 74 automated tests, run against real NASA and SoilGrids data.
  • Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

How it’s creative

  • The pump is also a sensor. Its record of every run becomes evidence about soil health: over-watering that washes nutrients away shows up in the soil score.
  • Pumping timed to the forecast sun. It plans a battery-less solar pump around tomorrow’s clouds, not a fixed timer.
  • Advice the farmer can actually follow. Crop rotation is checked against what this farmer’s own pump can deliver, not just what grows in the region.
  • NASA data where farmers already are. The data reaches them through a pump they pay for with M-Pesa every day, not through a separate dashboard.
  • A voice assistant that speaks Kiswahili and works out farm words the phone mishears.

Factors we considered

  • Affordability: pay-as-you-go, no diesel, and a controller built locally.
  • Connectivity: Bluetooth at the pump, paid time stored on the board, and answers and maps saved on the phone for when there’s no signal.
  • Literacy and language: plain words, voice input and read-aloud answers, Kiswahili, and one instruction instead of charts.
  • Honesty about data: forecasts and map values are labelled as estimates. The controller has no flow meter yet, so litres are estimated from run time and the pump’s flow rate, and we say so. We never give lime or fertiliser amounts without a soil test.
  • Gaps in the data: NASA POWER runs a few days behind, so the model fills the gap and says so. The soil map is blank over towns, so the app reads the land about 3 km around and tells the farmer. Climate temperatures are adjusted for the farm’s altitude.
  • Security and fairness: no API keys inside the app, prices set on the server, and paid credit that can’t be rolled back by resetting the board.
  • Local fit: Kenyan crops such as maize, beans, sukuma wiki (kale), and ndengu (green gram), M-Pesa payments, and Kiswahili.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
NASA POWER Daily API: temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation, rainfall, root-zone soil wetness
NASA POWER Climatology API: 25-year monthly averages
NASA SRTM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission) elevation
NASA SRTMGL3 v003: 90 m elevation data
